prompt.context: Our client is a small auto-parts manufacturer (APM Co.) with roughly $350M in revenue and operations on two continents. The company has experienced extreme growth in recent years, and the CEO is becoming pressured to improve profit margins to be more in line with competitors.
prompt.question: She wants us to help identify and implement improvements. How would you approach this problem?

clarifying_info.q: Can the company raise prices or sell more volume?
clarifying_info.a: Prices and quantities are contractually set in advance. The company has little-to-no ability to improve the top line in the short run.

clarifying_info.q: Is there a specific financial target for margin improvement?
clarifying_info.a: No specific target — they want as much improvement as fast as possible.

clarifying_info.q: How did the company grow and why might operations be inefficient?
clarifying_info.a: The company has grown through both organic and inorganic means. Because it has grown so quickly, staff have had limited time to share best practices and analyze operations for flaws. They are rushing to get orders out.
Plants are in Michigan, Tennessee, and Tianjin, China. MI and TN sell directly to OEMs. The CN plant does some such sales but mostly builds smaller components sold to manufacturers.
Primary customers are major US OEMs for MI and TN, and Tier 1 or Tier 2 suppliers for CN.

clarifying_info.q: How long do product contracts typically run?
clarifying_info.a: Typically a product will run at contractual levels for 5 years. After that, the company produces small batches for warranty.

exhibits.title: Company Financials by Manufacturing Facility
exhibits.shows: A financial summary table comparing all three manufacturing facilities (Michigan, Tennessee, China) across key income statement line items
exhibits.data: Revenue, cost of goods sold, gross profit, operating expenses broken down by facility; allows comparison of margins and cost structures across the three plants

exhibits.title: Financials for Tennessee Facility by Line
exhibits.shows: A detailed P&L breakdown for the Tennessee facility, showing financial data by individual production line and specific cost categories
exhibits.data: Line-level revenue and costs for the TN plant; includes scrap, freight, overhead, and workers compensation line items that allow identification of problem areas

exhibits.title: Cumulative Scrap Rate by Manufacturing Step — Line A
exhibits.shows: A bar or table showing the contribution of each manufacturing step to total scrap on Line A, plus the investment required to reduce scrap spend by 80% at each step
exhibits.data: Steps: Clean (0% contribution, N/A investment), Re-form (2.5% contribution, $2.5M investment), Attach (90% contribution, $5.5M investment), Trim (2.5% contribution, $2.5M investment), Cure (1.25% contribution, $1.5M investment), Coat (3.75% contribution, $4.0M investment); investment figures represent cost to reduce scrap at that step by 80%

exhibits.title: Tennessee Line A: Supply Chain Network & Spend by Segment
exhibits.shows: A network diagram of the supply chain feeding Tennessee Line A, with freight spend labeled on each segment between the Chinese facility, supplier, and the Tennessee facility
exhibits.data: Segment spend amounts: $1,800k, $460k, $380k, $170k, $320k, $80k; note states that the Chinese route accounts for 100% of $1.1M in expedited freight for Line A

framework: Logistics — Non-optimized order quantities, Redundant supply routes, Expensive routes and modes
Procurement — Expensive sourcing, Poor demand forecasting, Lack of balance between inventory and freight costs

questions.prompt: After reviewing Exhibit 1, which plant would you prioritize and why?
questions.guidance: A strong candidate identifies Tennessee as the priority based on comparatively poor margins across scrap, freight, overhead, and workers comp. Michigan should be noted as less urgent because it is the primary R&D center — its lower apparent profit is explained by R&D spend critical to the company. China has lower labor and overhead costs typical for that geography. Tennessee shows four red flags simultaneously: high scrap, high freight, high overhead, and high workers comp/safety costs. If the candidate focuses on Michigan, probe whether they notice R&D before redirecting to Tennessee.

questions.prompt: From the Tennessee financials (Exhibit 2), what are the main areas for improvement and which would you tackle first?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify four main cost areas: scrap, freight, overhead, and workers comp/safety. If they want to focus on labor, overhead, or workers comp, note that these will take a few years to address due to union negotiations. Scrap and freight are actionable immediately. Scrap has a higher sticker-price saving, so it is a logical first focus. A very strong candidate gets through both scrap and freight; an extremely strong candidate also raises overhead and workers comp.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 3, evaluate whether APM Co. should invest $5.5M in a new 'attach machine' to reduce scrap on Line A.
questions.guidance: Candidate must identify that the Attach step drives 90% of scrap, calculate annual scrap savings from the investment, derive the payback period, and judge whether it is worthwhile given the 5-year contract (product is in year 1 of 5, so ~2 years payback leaves ~3 years of benefit). No discount rates are applied.

math.setup: Total Line A scrap (from TN financials) = $3.7M per year. Attach step = 90% of total scrap. Investment reduces attach scrap by 80%. Payback = Investment / Annual Savings. Product is in year 1 of 5 (no discount rate).
math.answer: Payback ~2.1 years against a remaining 4-year contract window — this is a good investment. Should move forward.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 4, diagnose the freight problem on Line A and evaluate the options to reduce expedited freight costs.
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify that the China-to-Tennessee segment accounts for 100% of the $1.1M expedited freight. Root cause: the Chinese JV is running hand-to-mouth (barely meets demand, ships by expedited air immediately). Brainstorm solutions: increase capacity at the JV, resource to another facility (not possible — OEM approval takes too long), increase employee hours (not possible — already near 24/7), outsource (possible but client concerned about IP). After brainstorming, candidate should evaluate switching from expedited air to sea freight by investing in capacity, using the provided math. Inventory holding cost = 20%; product is in year 1 of 5. Formula: 12 × (change in monthly spend) − 0.20 × (change in average inventory).

math.setup: Current monthly freight spend vs. sea scenario monthly spend. Current average inventory vs. sea scenario average inventory. Holding cost = 20% of average inventory. Net annual benefit = 12 × ΔMonthly Spend − 0.20 × ΔAvgInventory. (Note: inventory increases under sea shipping because shipping frequency drops from every 2 days to every 1–2 months.)
math.answer: Switching to sea freight (with capacity investment) saves approximately $0.83M per year net of increased inventory holding costs.

brainstorming.prompt: What options exist to address the hand-to-mouth situation at the Chinese JV supplying Line A?

categories.name: Capacity expansion
ideas: Invest in additional equipment at the Chinese JV to increase output and allow batch shipping
Add a second shift or additional production lines

categories.name: Alternative sourcing
ideas: Resource component to another facility (caveat: OEMs must approve — takes too long in near term)
Outsource to a third-party manufacturer (caveat: client concerned about IP leakage)

categories.name: Labor hours
ideas: Increase employee hours (caveat: facility already operating close to 24/7 — not feasible)

categories.name: Inventory / logistics restructuring
ideas: Build safety stock buffer to allow switch from air to sea freight
Negotiate longer lead times with the OEM customer to reduce expedite pressure

recommendation: APMC can immediately improve margins on Line A in Tennessee by investing in a new attach machine, which will reduce scrap costs by approximately $2.66M per year with a payback period of ~2 years
Simultaneously, investing in capacity at the Chinese JV will allow a switch from expedited air to sea shipments, saving approximately $0.83M per year net of increased inventory holding costs
risks: Switching to sea shipments increases inventory levels, raising the risk of markdowns or obsolescence if demand changes
Sea shipments increase the risk of lost or damaged goods in transit

Widespread problems at Tennessee (high scrap, freight, overhead, and workers comp simultaneously) may indicate underlying leadership or management challenges, suggesting these fixes are only short-term solutions
next_steps: Complete the attach machine purchase for Line A
Invest in Chinese JV capacity to enable the shift to sea freight
Ensure shipping insurance is in place for sea route
Explore management training or leadership improvements at the Tennessee facility
Examine opportunities to reduce overhead costs at Tennessee
Investigate the extremely high workers compensation numbers at Tennessee as a potential safety and cost issue
